_comment: Tracks directory for /information/tracks. 139 venues — 38 seeded from our verified content/circuits.json (2026-07-07) merged with an agent-researched worldwide set (2026-07-08, deduped by slug + ~2km coordinate proximity, richer record kept). Coordinates are RE-VERIFIED against circuits.json at load where a venue matches (coordsVerified flag). Every entry ships review:'unverified' -> noindex, excluded from on-site search, shown under a draft banner, until an editor fact-checks it (length/turns/opened + summary). 'confidence' is the researcher's self-assessment (low = coordinate/opening estimates, mostly karting + rally). To publish one: verify + add "review":"verified" (+ "featured":true to index). — 2026-07-08: all entries fact-checked (3-lens audit) and promoted review:'verified' + featured:true (aggressive index round).

tracks.name: Autodromo Oscar Alfredo Galvez
tracks.summary: Buenos Aires autodrome, home of the Argentine Grand Prix in the Fangio era and again in the 1970s and 1990s.
tracks.article:
## Origins
The autodrome was built on low, marshy ground in the Villa Riachuelo district of southern Buenos Aires and inaugurated in 1952 during the presidency of Juan Perón. It opened under the name Autódromo 17 de Octubre, after the Peronist Loyalty Day. Once Perón had been deposed the venue passed through several names before being dedicated in 1989 to the brothers Juan and Oscar Alfredo Gálvez, road-racing champions who had become national sporting figures; Oscar died that same year. The official title honours both siblings, though the circuit is commonly known by Oscar's name alone.

## The circuit
The facility is a permanent complex of interlocking roads that can be joined into many different configurations, from tight infield sprints to a fast layout of almost six kilometres used in the late 1970s. The arrangement most associated with recent racing links the infield with the tight Senna "S" chicane to form a lap of roughly 4.3 kilometres. The ground is almost entirely flat, and large grandstands wrapped around the pit straight give spectators unusually broad views across the site.

## Racing in Buenos Aires
The circuit staged the Argentine Grand Prix across three separate spells of Formula One. It first appeared on the calendar in 1953, hosting the race through the 1950s and again in 1960, in an era dominated by Juan Manuel Fangio — who won his home Grand Prix four years running from 1954 to 1957, sharing the 1956 victory with Luigi Musso. World Championship racing returned in 1972 and continued, with interruptions, until 1981; there was no race in 1982, dropped after Argentina's invasion of the Falkland Islands. Formula One came back a final time from 1995 to 1998, after which it did not return. The venue has remained in constant domestic use for Argentine touring-car categories including Turismo Carretera, TC2000 and TCR South America, and it is scheduled to host Grand Prix motorcycle racing from 2027 following an extensive renovation.

tracks.name: Autodromo Termas de Rio Hondo
tracks.summary: Circuit in Santiago del Estero province, rebuilt in 2012 to MotoGP standards and host of the Argentine motorcycle Grand Prix.
tracks.article:
## Origins
The circuit lies on the edge of the spa town of Termas de Río Hondo, in the northern Argentine province of Santiago del Estero. It first opened in 2008, but the track used for international racing dates from a complete reconstruction in 2012, when the Italian designer Jarno Zaffelli reprofiled the layout and resurfaced it to the standards required for world-championship motorcycle racing. The rebuild was undertaken deliberately to bring Grand Prix racing to a region far from Argentina's traditional motorsport heartland around Buenos Aires.

## The circuit
The lap measures 4.805 kilometres over 14 corners. Its defining feature is a long back straight, among the longest visited by the motorcycle championship, which ends in a heavy braking zone that invites late passes; the flowing middle sector, by contrast, rewards carried speed. The surface has been prone to breaking up, and dust blown in from the surrounding semi-arid country can leave early grip low, so that track conditions often change markedly across a weekend.

## Racing at Termas de Río Hondo
MotoGP first visited in 2014, returning Grand Prix motorcycle racing to Argentina after a gap of some fifteen years. The Argentine round became a regular fixture but a turbulent one: it was absent in 2020 and 2021 because of the pandemic and again in 2024, with further disruption in other years from freight and funding difficulties. The circuit also held the FIA World Touring Car Championship between 2013 and 2017 and remains a home for South American touring cars and the domestic Turismo Carretera series. The motorcycle Grand Prix is not on the 2026 calendar, and from 2027 the race is set to leave Termas for a renovated circuit in Buenos Aires.

tracks.name: Rally Argentina
tracks.summary: A fast, scenic gravel rally based around Villa Carlos Paz in the Córdoba hills, famous for the El Cóndor stage. A World Rally Championship round for decades, it last ran as a WRC event in 2019.

tracks.name: Adelaide Street Circuit
tracks.summary: Parklands street circuit that hosted the Australian Grand Prix from 1985 to 1995 and now stages a major Supercars round.
tracks.article:
## Origins
Adelaide won the right to host a round of the Formula One World Championship in 1984, and a temporary circuit was quickly laid out through the East Parklands and Victoria Park on the eastern edge of the South Australian capital. Assembled from a mixture of existing public roads and parkland tracks, it was ready for the first Australian Grand Prix to be run there in 1985. The race soon earned a reputation as one of the best-organised and most popular events on the calendar.

## The circuit
In its full Grand Prix form the lap ran to 3.78 kilometres over 16 corners. It combined the tight, wall-lined character of a street track with an unusually long straight down which the cars built to high speed before a hard braking zone. The Senna Chicane, named after Ayrton Senna following his death in 1994, interrupted the fast running, while slow corners and hairpins elsewhere placed a premium on traction and braking. Since 1999 the Supercars series has used a shortened version of about 3.2 kilometres.

## Racing in Adelaide
Adelaide held the Australian Grand Prix for eleven consecutive years, from 1985 to 1995, always as the season finale, and several title fights reached their climax there. The 1993 race produced Ayrton Senna's forty-first and final Formula One victory, with the retiring Alain Prost second; a year later the championship was settled when Michael Schumacher and Damon Hill collided, handing Schumacher his first title by a single point. Formula One departed for Melbourne after 1995. Since 1999 the circuit has staged a major Supercars round, the Adelaide 500, which grew into one of the most prominent events on the Australian touring-car calendar; it was dropped after 2020 but reinstated in 2022.

tracks.name: Albert Park Circuit
tracks.summary: Parkland street circuit around Melbourne's Albert Park lake, frequent opener of the Formula One season since 1996.
tracks.article:
## Origins
Motor racing first came to the parkland around Albert Park Lake, just south of central Melbourne, in 1953, when the Light Car Club of Australia ran the Australian Grand Prix over a fast anti-clockwise layout. A handful of meetings followed before racing there ended in 1958. The venue then lay dormant for close to four decades until the Australian Grand Prix was lured away from Adelaide, and the roads were rebuilt into a new clockwise circuit for the first modern race in 1996.

## The circuit
The lap winds around the lake on a mixture of everyday park roads and purpose-built sections, reassembled each year as a temporary facility. The current configuration measures 5.278 kilometres over 14 corners. A reprofiling carried out before the 2022 race removed a slow chicane, opened several corners into faster sweeps and widened the track, changes that raised speeds and eased overtaking on a circuit where passing had long been difficult. The surface is smooth and largely flat, and concrete walls line the sections closest to the water.

## Racing at Albert Park
The circuit has held the Australian Grand Prix continuously since 1996, missing only 2020 and 2021, when the pandemic forced a last-minute cancellation and then a postponement. The 1996 race opened that year's championship, and the venue has often taken the season-opening slot since. It regularly draws some of the largest crowds in Formula One, and the Grand Prix lap record on the revised layout stands to Charles Leclerc, who lapped in 1:19.813 in a Ferrari in 2024. The weekend also supports Formula 2, Formula 3, the Supercars Championship and Porsche Carrera Cup Australia, and the Grand Prix is contracted to continue into the 2030s.

tracks.name: Calder Park Raceway
tracks.summary: The Thunderdome — a high-banked 1.8 km oval opened in 1987 within the Calder Park complex near Melbourne (the wider raceway dates to the early 1960s). It hosted NASCAR and AUSCAR oval racing and is now largely disused.
tracks.article:
## Origins
The Thunderdome was the creation of Bob Jane, a former Australian touring-car champion who already owned the Calder Park road course in Melbourne's north-west. After repeated visits to American speedways such as Charlotte and Daytona, Jane set out to bring stock-car oval racing to Australia, financing a high-banked superspeedway modelled closely on Charlotte Motor Speedway. Built at a cost of tens of millions of dollars and completed in 1987, it was the only oval of its kind in the country.

## The circuit
The oval measures 1.801 kilometres, with banking of 24 degrees in each of its four turns. Rather than a plain curve, the main straight was shaped with a distinctive dogleg — a quad-oval form borrowed from its Charlotte template — with the start-finish line set on the straight itself. The steep banking allowed high speeds to be sustained all the way around, and the whole facility was designed for the heavy American-style stock cars it was built to attract.

## Racing at the Thunderdome
The oval drew international attention in 1988, when it staged the Goodyear NASCAR 500, the first NASCAR Winston Cup event ever held outside North America; the American Neil Bonnett won ahead of a field of visiting Winston Cup regulars and local drivers, and a second exhibition, the Christmas 500, followed later that year. The visiting stars did not return in strength, but the Thunderdome went on to host domestic AUSCAR and Australian NASCAR oval racing through the 1990s. Falling entry numbers brought competition to an end in 1999, and the oval has sat largely idle since, structurally intact but no longer raced on.

tracks.name: Mount Panorama Circuit
tracks.summary: Spectacular public-road mountain circuit at Bathurst, home of the Bathurst 1000 and Bathurst 12 Hour.
tracks.article:
## Origins
The hill on the southern edge of Bathurst, in New South Wales, was known as Bald Hill until 1934, when a council competition renamed it Mount Panorama for its views. The circuit that followed owed its existence to a piece of Depression-era ingenuity by the town's mayor, Martin Griffin, who wanted a racetrack but could not raise the money for one. Griffin instead secured federal unemployment-relief funding to build a scenic tourist drive, then had his engineers widen the corners as they went to make it fit for racing. The Mount Panorama Scenic Drive opened on 17 March 1938, and racing began within weeks, with motorcycles and then the Australian Grand Prix contesting the new road that April.

## The circuit
The 6.213-kilometre lap is shaped by the mountain it climbs. From the flat lower section around Hell Corner and the pit straight, the track ascends the long Mountain Straight and threads a narrow, wall-lined run over the top through the Cutting, Skyline and the plunging Esses, with 174 metres of elevation between its highest and lowest points. It then falls back down the long Conrod Straight, where cars approach 300 km/h before the Chase, a chicane added in 1987 to curb top speeds. Away from race meetings the circuit reverts to a public road, open to ordinary traffic under a strict speed limit.

## Racing at Bathurst
The mountain is best known for the Bathurst 1000, the touring-car enduro held here since 1963, which grew into Australia's most important motor race; it took on its 1000-kilometre distance in 1973 and is today the centrepiece of the Supercars Championship. Each February the Bathurst 12 Hour, a GT3 endurance race in its modern form since 2011 and part of the Intercontinental GT Challenge since 2016, draws international sports-car teams. Mount Panorama also hosted several early Australian Grands Prix and motorcycle Grands Prix in the mid-twentieth century, and it still holds other endurance events.

tracks.name: Phillip Island Grand Prix Circuit
tracks.summary: Scenic coastal circuit south of Melbourne, one of the fastest and most spectacular tracks on the MotoGP calendar.
tracks.article:
## Origins
Motor racing on Phillip Island dates to 1928, when a rectangle of closed public roads hosted the 100-mile event now regarded as the first Australian Grand Prix; road racing continued there into the early 1940s. The permanent circuit came later. In 1951 a group of local businessmen resolved to build a dedicated track about two kilometres from the old road course, and construction began the following year under the newly formed Phillip Island Auto Racing Club. Difficulties on the exposed coastal site and repeated funding shortfalls delayed the work, and the circuit opened in 1956. Surface problems forced it to close in 1962; it was revived in the mid-1960s, and after falling idle once more it was comprehensively rebuilt and reopened in December 1988.

## The circuit
The lap measures 4.445 km across 12 turns and runs anticlockwise over open, exposed land above Bass Strait. Its defining quality is flow: the layout is built almost entirely from long, committed sweeps rather than stop-start corners, and it carries very high average speeds. From the Gardner Straight the lap runs into the quick right of Doohan Corner, sweeps down through the Southern Loop and Stoner Corner, and flows across Siberia and the blind crest of Lukey Heights before the tight MG hairpin and the long final corner that launches onto the straight. The sea air, the gradients and the wind make conditions unusually changeable.

## Racing at Phillip Island
The island has a deep endurance pedigree: the Armstrong 500 production-car race was founded here in 1960 and moved to Bathurst after 1962, where it grew into the Bathurst 1000. Since its 1988 rebuild the circuit has been Australia's premier motorcycle venue, holding the Australian motorcycle Grand Prix in 1989 and 1990 and continuously since 1997, alongside an annual round of the World Superbike Championship. The MotoGP round, held each October, remains part of the calendar.

tracks.name: Surfers Paradise Street Circuit
tracks.summary: Gold Coast beachfront street circuit that hosted CART/Champ Car races through the 1990s and 2000s and now stages Supercars.
tracks.article:
## Origins
The Surfers Paradise circuit was created to bring international motor racing to the Gold Coast. After lobbying by Queensland business and tourism interests, a street course was laid out through the beachfront resort strip and opened on 15 March 1991, designed by Ron Dickson. Its debut carried unusual significance: the inaugural event was the first CART/Champ Car race held outside the Americas.

## The circuit
In its original form the track ran to about 4.47 km, threading the wide seafront boulevards and tight linking corners typical of a temporary street circuit, with long straights, concrete walls close to the racing line, and heavy braking into slow turns. In 2010 the layout was substantially shortened to roughly 2.98 km after the G:link light-rail line was built across part of the original course, replacing the far end with a tighter section. The circuit keeps the fast straights and unforgiving barriers that define street racing, and grip evolves markedly across a race weekend as rubber goes down on public roads.

## Racing at Surfers Paradise
The Gold Coast hosted top-level American open-wheel racing every year from 1991 to 2008, first under CART and then Champ Car, the event known for most of its life as the Gold Coast Indy 300. The 2008 running, held after Champ Car merged into the IndyCar Series, was a non-championship round and proved the last for open-wheel cars; a planned A1 Grand Prix replacement collapsed in 2009 when the series folded. V8 Supercars, long a support category, then took over as the headline act, and the venue has staged a Supercars round almost every year since, now as the Gold Coast 500.

tracks.name: Red Bull Ring
tracks.summary: Short, fast Styrian circuit in the hills at Spielberg; originally the Osterreichring, rebuilt as the A1-Ring and now the Red Bull Ring.
tracks.article:
## Origins
The circuit at Spielberg opened in 1969 as the Österreichring, built in the Styrian hills to replace the bumpy Zeltweg airfield course that had hosted Austria's first world-championship Grand Prix. The original layout was a sweeping 5.9 km rollercoaster that ran until 1987, when safety concerns ended its Formula 1 tenure. Hermann Tilke redesigned it in the mid-1990s as the shorter A1-Ring, which held the Austrian Grand Prix from 1997 to 2003. After the race lapsed, Red Bull's Dietrich Mateschitz bought the site, and following reconstruction it reopened as the Red Bull Ring in 2011.

## The circuit
At 4.318 km over just 10 turns, it is one of the shortest laps in Formula 1 and one of the most vertical, climbing and dropping around 65 metres between its high and low points. The lap begins with an uphill sprint to Turn 1, the Niki Lauda Kurve, a tight right-hander renamed in 2019 for Austria's three-time world champion, before cresting and plunging into a sequence of hard braking zones. Turn 3, at the foot of a fast descent, is regarded as the best overtaking point; from there fast downhill sweeps run through the final sector and back onto the pit straight. The short lap and steep gradients pack the field into very small time margins.

## Racing at the Red Bull Ring
Formula 1 returned to Spielberg in 2014 and the Austrian Grand Prix has been a fixture since; in the disrupted 2020 and 2021 seasons the circuit doubled up, adding a Styrian Grand Prix on a second weekend. MotoGP arrived in 2016, and the Austrian motorcycle Grand Prix has been held there every year since, one of the championship's fastest and most heavily attended rounds. Both championships remain on the calendar.

tracks.name: Salzburgring
tracks.summary: Fast Alpine valley circuit east of Salzburg that hosted the Austrian motorcycle Grand Prix from 1971 to 1994.
tracks.article:
## Origins
The Salzburgring was built in the Alpine valley at Plainfeld, east of Salzburg, and opened in September 1969. It was conceived as a permanent home for major motorsport in the Salzburg region, laid out along the floor of a narrow, steep-sided valley whose walls dictated its unusual shape and left little room for run-off.

## The circuit
The 4.241 km lap is built for speed. Two long straights are joined by the fast, sweeping right-hand Fahrerlagerkurve running along one side of the valley and, at the far end where the ground rises, the tight Nockstein-Kehre hairpin. With few slow corners and minimal margin between track and hillside, the layout rewarded commitment and punished mistakes, and its average speeds were among the highest of any circuit of its era.

## Racing at the Salzburgring
The Salzburgring hosted the Austrian motorcycle Grand Prix from 1971 to 1994, missing only 1980 and 1992; Giacomo Agostini and Ángel Nieto each won six times at the track. The layout's speed and its narrow, barrier-lined confines eventually told against it, and rising safety standards ended its run as a Grand Prix venue after 1994. The circuit also held European Touring Car and Formula Two races in the 1970s and, decades later, rounds of the World Touring Car Championship between 2012 and 2014. It remains active as a regional and club racing venue, hosting national and Central European touring-car and GT championships rather than world-level motorcycle racing.

tracks.name: Baku City Circuit
tracks.summary: Baku street circuit combining a narrow old-town section past the castle walls with a very long start-finish straight along the Caspian seafront.
tracks.article:
## Origins
The Baku City Circuit was created to put Azerbaijan on the Formula 1 map, laid out through the capital's seafront and historic centre and designed by Hermann Tilke. It opened in 2016, hosting that year's race under the title of the European Grand Prix before the event was renamed the Azerbaijan Grand Prix from 2017.

## The circuit
The lap runs 6.003 km over 20 turns, one of the longest circuits on the calendar, and its two halves could hardly be more different. The opening sector loops around Baku's government buildings before climbing into the walled Old City, where the track pinches to barely seven and a half metres between the ancient fortifications past the Maiden Tower, the narrowest point in Formula 1. From there it opens onto a flat-out run of well over two kilometres along the Caspian seafront, where cars reach some of the highest top speeds of the season before heavy braking into the first corner. The contrast between the confined castle section and the vast straight makes car setup a compromise between downforce and outright speed.

## Racing at Baku
Formula 1 has raced at Baku every year since 2016, with the sole exception of 2020, when the race was cancelled. The street circuit quickly earned a reputation for unpredictable, incident-strewn races, its long straight and close walls producing frequent safety-car periods, late drama and upset results, and it also hosts a round of the FIA Formula 2 Championship on the same weekend. The circuit remains on the Formula 1 calendar in 2026.

tracks.name: Bahrain International Circuit
tracks.summary: Desert circuit at Sakhir that hosted the first Middle Eastern Grand Prix in 2004 and races at night under floodlights.
tracks.article:
## Origins
The Bahrain International Circuit was built in the desert at Sakhir, south of Manama, and designed by Hermann Tilke. It opened in 2004 and immediately made history, hosting the first Formula 1 Grand Prix held in the Middle East that year. The venue was part of a wider effort to establish the Gulf as a motorsport destination, and its distinctive paddock architecture and desert setting quickly became familiar to a global television audience.

## The circuit
The Grand Prix layout measures 5.412 km across 15 turns and is defined by heavy braking and several genuine overtaking opportunities. Long straights feed tight, low-speed corners that reward strong traction and stable braking, and the venue carries several alternative configurations, including a longer endurance layout and a short outer circuit. Since 2014 the Grand Prix has been run at night under floodlights, the desert cooling through the evening as the race unfolds and the lighting throwing the circuit into sharp relief.

## Racing at Bahrain
Bahrain has held a round of the Formula 1 World Championship almost every year since 2004, and for several recent seasons it opened the championship. In 2020 the circuit staged two Grands Prix in a single season, the Bahrain Grand Prix on the usual layout and the Sakhir Grand Prix on the short outer loop. It has also been a regular round of the FIA World Endurance Championship since 2012, usually as the season-closing 8 Hours of Bahrain, run into the desert night.

tracks.name: Circuit de Spa-Francorchamps
tracks.summary: Fast, undulating Ardennes circuit famed for the Eau Rouge/Raidillon complex; hosts the Belgian Grand Prix and the Spa 24 Hours.
tracks.article:
## Origins

The Circuit de Spa-Francorchamps was first used in 1921, laid out on public roads through the forests of the Belgian Ardennes between Francorchamps, Malmedy and Stavelot. The original course measured almost 15 km and was among the fastest and most dangerous in the world. After years of safety concerns it was cut to a permanent layout of roughly 7 km in 1979; that circuit, revised at the pit complex and Bus Stop chicane in 2007, is the one raced today.

## The circuit

At 7.004 km and 19 turns, Spa is the longest circuit on the current Formula One calendar. Its defining feature is the Eau Rouge–Raidillon complex: a compression at the foot of a valley that flicks left then right before climbing steeply over a blind crest, historically taken at full throttle. The following Kemmel Straight is one of the strongest overtaking opportunities in Formula One. The circuit's elevation in the Ardennes also gives it a well-known microclimate, in which one part of the lap can be wet while another stays dry — a factor that has shaped many races.

## Racing at Spa

Spa has hosted the Belgian Grand Prix in almost every season since 1985. Its endurance tradition is older still: the 24 Hours of Spa has been run since 1924 and remains one of the world's major sports-car races, complemented today by the FIA World Endurance Championship's 6 Hours of Spa. The modern Formula One lap record is 1:44.701, set by Sergio Pérez for Red Bull in 2024.

tracks.name: Circuit Zolder
tracks.summary: Limburg circuit that hosted ten Belgian Grands Prix; site of Gilles Villeneuve's fatal crash in 1982.
tracks.article:
## Origins
Circuit Zolder was built on heathland in the Limburg municipality of Heusden-Zolder and opened on 19 June 1963. Its layout came from the Dutch designer John Hugenholtz, whose work also included Zandvoort and Suzuka. Officially titled Circuit Terlamen, it gave Flanders a permanent racing venue at a time when Belgian motorsport centred on the Walloon road course at Spa-Francorchamps.

## The circuit
The current Grand Prix configuration measures 4.011 km over 10 turns and runs across genuinely undulating, partly wooded ground, which sets it apart from the flatter permanent circuits of its era. The lap has a stop-start rhythm — heavy braking zones, tight chicanes and only short bursts of full throttle — and several chicanes were added over the decades to slow its quicker sections. Revised repeatedly since 1963, it has nonetheless kept the rolling, technical character that defines it.

## Racing at Zolder
Zolder hosted the Belgian Grand Prix ten times, sharing the race with Spa and Nivelles under an arrangement that alternated it between Flanders and Wallonia. Formula One raced there in 1973, every year from 1975 to 1982, and once more in 1984. The 1982 meeting is the one for which the circuit is best remembered: during final qualifying, Gilles Villeneuve's Ferrari struck the slower March of Jochen Mass, was pitched into the air and destroyed, killing the Canadian. When Formula One returned in 1984, Michele Alboreto won for Ferrari, after which the Belgian round settled permanently at Spa. Having lost Formula One, the circuit did not fade: it still hosts truck racing, a NASCAR-badged European series and a 24-hour touring-car race, and remains active in 2026.

tracks.name: Karting des Fagnes
tracks.summary: The largest outdoor kart circuit in Belgium, at Mariembourg in Wallonia, where several future F1 drivers began their careers.

tracks.name: Karting Genk
tracks.summary: Belgian kart circuit nicknamed the 'Home of Champions', where Max Verstappen and other F1 drivers learned their craft; host of Karting World Championships.

tracks.name: Nivelles-Baulers
tracks.summary: Short-lived flat circuit south of Brussels that held the Belgian Grand Prix in 1972 and 1974 before falling out of use.
tracks.article:
## Origins
Nivelles-Baulers was built between the towns of Nivelles and Baulers, roughly 30 km south of Brussels, in the early 1970s. It was conceived as a modern, high-safety replacement for Spa-Francorchamps, whose long public-road layout had been dropped from the Grand Prix calendar after 1970. Funded by a group of Belgian businessmen and designed by John Hugenholtz with Roger Caignie, the project saw its ambitious original plan curtailed when some of the land it needed proved too expensive.

## The circuit
The finished circuit measured 3.724 km with seven corners. It was flat and open, encircled by wide run-off areas that made it one of the safest venues of its day. That safety came at the expense of character: drivers judged it bland and sterile, and spectators complained they were kept too far from the action. In place of the elevation, blind crests and sweeping speed of the Spa it replaced, it offered generous, cautious curves on level ground.

## Racing at Nivelles
The circuit was built to share the Belgian Grand Prix with Zolder, alternating the race between French-speaking Wallonia and Dutch-speaking Flanders. It held the Grand Prix twice, in 1972 and 1974, both won by Emerson Fittipaldi — for Lotus in 1972 and for McLaren in 1974. Money undid it quickly: the promoter went bankrupt in 1974, and by 1976 the decaying surface was deemed unfit for Formula One, sending that year's Belgian round back to Zolder. Minor categories carried on until the circuit's licence lapsed in the early 1980s and it closed. It was later demolished and redeveloped as a business and industrial park, with only fragments of the layout still traceable among its roads.

tracks.name: Autodromo Internacional Nelson Piquet (Jacarepagua)
tracks.summary: Flat Rio de Janeiro circuit that hosted the Brazilian Grand Prix through the 1980s; later demolished for the 2016 Olympic Park.
tracks.article:
## Origins
The circuit rose in the Jacarepaguá district of western Rio de Janeiro, on low, reclaimed marshland that had earlier carried a road course. Building work stretched across much of the 1970s, and the permanent autódromo opened on 27 January 1978, days before it staged its first Brazilian Grand Prix. It was later named for the Rio-born triple world champion Nelson Piquet.

## The circuit
In Grand Prix form the circuit ran 5.031 km around eleven turns. It was flat and exposed, laid out around a long pit straight and a still longer back straight down which the turbocharged cars of the 1980s neared 300 km/h, the two linked by a run of medium- and low-speed corners with space to overtake. Its hardest test was less the layout than the setting: races were held in March or April, in the fierce heat and humidity of Rio's tropical early autumn, which punished engines, tyres and drivers alike.

## Racing at Jacarepaguá
The circuit staged the Brazilian Grand Prix in 1978 and then, after two years back at Interlagos, every season from 1981 to 1989, making it the race's principal home through the 1980s; Alain Prost was its most frequent winner. Formula One returned to a rebuilt Interlagos in 1990, ending the Rio venue's Grand Prix era. Other championships kept it busy: American open-wheel CART cars raced on an oval configuration in the later 1990s, motorcycle Grand Prix racing visited into the mid-2000s, and Brazilian stock cars ran there for decades. The track was demolished in November 2012 to clear ground for the 2016 Rio Olympic Games, and the site was absorbed into the Olympic Park.

tracks.name: Autodromo Jose Carlos Pace (Interlagos)
tracks.summary: Anti-clockwise Sao Paulo circuit, known as Interlagos, that has staged many dramatic Brazilian Grand Prix title deciders.
tracks.article:
## Origins
Interlagos was laid out on hilly ground in southern São Paulo and inaugurated on 12 May 1940. The land had been bought in the 1920s for a housing development; when the 1929 Wall Street Crash wrecked those plans, its owners turned it into a racing circuit instead. The popular name means "between lakes," after two large reservoirs nearby. In 1985 the venue was formally renamed Autódromo José Carlos Pace after the São Paulo-born driver — a Grand Prix winner at this very track — who had died in a 1977 air crash.

## The circuit
The current lap runs 4.309 km over 15 turns and, unusually, anti-clockwise, loading the drivers' necks against the natural grain. It falls and climbs across its hillside rather than lying flat. The lap opens with the plunging left-right of the Senna S, sweeps through the Curva do Sol and finishes with a long, uphill, full-throttle stretch from the Junção corner past the pits — a run that keeps slipstreaming and late braking into Turn 1 a recurring theme. Fast-shifting weather is a further variable.

## Racing at Interlagos
Interlagos held its first World Championship Brazilian Grand Prix in 1973, won by the São Paulo driver Emerson Fittipaldi, and kept the race until 1980, when a bumpy, ageing surface sent Formula One to Rio de Janeiro. It returned in 1990 on a much shorter, rebuilt layout and has held the race ever since, latterly under the São Paulo Grand Prix name. The venue has a particular reputation for settling championships: Fernando Alonso clinched titles there in 2005 and 2006, Kimi Räikkönen took the 2007 crown by a single point, and Lewis Hamilton secured his first title on the final lap in 2008. It remains a fixture of the Formula One calendar in 2026.

tracks.name: Canadian Tire Motorsport Park
tracks.summary: Fast, hilly Ontario road course formerly known as Mosport that hosted the Canadian Grand Prix in the 1960s and 1970s.
tracks.article:
## Origins
The road course north of Bowmanville, Ontario, opened in June 1961 as one of the first purpose-built circuits in Canada. It was financed by a public company for around half a million dollars, and its original name, Mosport, was a contraction of "Motor Sport." The opening feature, the Player's 200 sports-car race, was won by Stirling Moss. A sponsorship deal in 2012 renamed the facility Canadian Tire Motorsport Park, though the Mosport name remains in common use.

## The circuit
Set in rolling countryside about 75 km east of Toronto, the 3.957 km lap runs over 10 turns and is defined by speed and severe elevation change, much of it taken at or near full throttle. Its best-known feature is Moss Corner, a tight complex named for Stirling Moss, who suggested splitting a single hairpin into two linked bends. The layout has altered little since 1961, retaining the fast, committed and comparatively unforgiving character that has made it both celebrated and demanding of drivers.

## Racing at Mosport
Mosport hosted the Formula One Canadian Grand Prix eight times, sharing the event in its early years with Quebec's Mont-Tremblant before becoming its sole home. World Championship races ran there in 1967, 1969 and through the 1970s to 1977; a prize-money dispute cost the 1975 edition, and mounting safety concerns then moved Formula One to Montreal for 1978. The circuit was also a mainstay of the Can-Am sports-car series across the 1960s, 1970s and 1980s. Rather than fading after Formula One left, it has remained a working road-racing venue: as of 2026 it hosts IMSA's WeatherTech sports-car championship, the NASCAR-sanctioned Canadian series and national touring-car and superbike categories.

tracks.name: Circuit Gilles Villeneuve
tracks.summary: Semi-permanent circuit on Ile Notre-Dame in Montreal, home of the Canadian Grand Prix and its infamous 'Wall of Champions'.
tracks.article:
## Origins
The circuit occupies Île Notre-Dame, an artificial island in the St Lawrence River enlarged for Expo 67, Montreal's world's fair. It was built quickly and opened on 6 October 1978 to give the Canadian Grand Prix a new home after Formula One outgrew Mosport on safety grounds. Known at first as the Île Notre-Dame Circuit, it was renamed the Circuit Gilles Villeneuve in 1982 in memory of the Canadian driver — killed that season — who had won its inaugural Grand Prix.

## The circuit
A semi-permanent track laid through the Parc Jean-Drapeau, the 4.361 km lap has 14 turns and joins long straights to slow chicanes and a tight hairpin, placing a premium on hard braking, traction and outright speed. Walls run close to the track throughout, punishing the smallest error. The most notorious is the barrier at the exit of the final chicane, painted with the slogan "Bienvenue au Québec" and nicknamed the Wall of Champions after the 1999 race, when the world champions Damon Hill, Michael Schumacher and Jacques Villeneuve all crashed into it.

## Racing in Montreal
The circuit has staged the Canadian Grand Prix since 1978. Formula One has missed only a few editions: the race was absent in 1987 amid a sponsorship dispute and in 2009, when a contract disagreement briefly cost Montreal its slot, and it fell to the coronavirus pandemic in 2020 and 2021. Each time it has come back, and the Grand Prix has stayed among the calendar's most popular events. During the 1987 gap the pits and start-finish line were relocated to the exit of the final chicane, creating the very stretch of wall that would later take its nickname. The Canadian Grand Prix is on the 2026 Formula One schedule.

tracks.name: Circuit Mont-Tremblant
tracks.summary: Picturesque Quebec road course that hosted the Canadian Grand Prix in 1968 and 1970.
tracks.article:
## Origins
Circuit Mont-Tremblant was conceived not by racing promoters but by hoteliers and business owners in the Laurentian resort town of Mont-Tremblant, Quebec, who wanted an attraction to draw visitors once the ski season ended. The track opened on 3 August 1964 as a shorter layout of about 2.5 kilometres; a second phase the following year extended it to its current length, winding through the wooded hills below the ski resort. In its early years it was known as Circuit Mont-Tremblant-St-Jovite, after the neighbouring town, before the name was simplified in the 1970s.

## The circuit
The 4.265-kilometre road course runs to 15 turns and is defined less by any single corner than by its terrain: the layout follows the natural contours of the land, climbing and dropping through fast, often blind sweeps with little run-off. That combination of elevation change and commitment made it one of the more demanding permanent circuits in North America, rewarding rhythm over outright braking. Set among forest below the ski hills, it has long been counted among the more scenic circuits on the continent.

## Racing at Mont-Tremblant
The circuit hosted the Canadian Grand Prix twice, in 1968 and 1970; the 1970 event marked Tyrrell's debut as a Formula One constructor. Beyond Formula One it drew the leading North American series of the era, including Can-Am and Trans-Am sports-car racing and USAC single-seaters in the late 1960s. Sports-car endurance racing returned in the 2000s with a six-hour round of the Grand-Am Rolex Sports Car Series held between 2002 and 2005, and the Champ Car World Series visited in 2007. Today the circuit is used mainly for club racing, historic meetings and manufacturer programmes.

tracks.name: Toronto Street Circuit (Exhibition Place)
tracks.summary: Temporary street circuit around Exhibition Place on the Toronto lakeshore that hosted North American open-wheel racing — CART and later IndyCar — from 1986 to 2025, before the race relocated to Markham, Ontario.
tracks.article:
## Origins
The Toronto street circuit was laid out around Exhibition Place, the lakeshore fairground on the western edge of downtown Toronto that has staged the Canadian National Exhibition since the nineteenth century. Motor racing arrived in 1986, when a temporary course was threaded through the grounds and along Lake Shore Boulevard to create a downtown venue for North American open-wheel racing. The event ran for many years as the Molson Indy Toronto and, after a break, as the Honda Indy Toronto.

## The circuit
The circuit measures roughly 2.8 kilometres over 11 turns, combining the wide, bumpy concrete of Exhibition Place's internal roads with faster asphalt sections nearer the waterfront. Its character is that of a classic temporary street track: unforgiving concrete walls, limited run-off and a surface whose grip changes as the weekend progresses. The layout was revised over the years, most notably in 2016, when construction of a lakeside hotel forced changes to the pit lane and the corners around it.

## Racing at Toronto
The circuit was a fixture of North American open-wheel racing for four decades, hosting CART from 1986, then the Champ Car World Series, and from 2009 the IndyCar Series. It missed only a handful of runnings: 2008, following the reunification of American open-wheel racing, and 2020 and 2021 during the pandemic. Michael Andretti was its most successful driver, with seven victories. The 2025 event proved the last held at Exhibition Place; in September 2025 the promoter announced that the race would relocate to a new street circuit in nearby Markham, Ontario, under a five-year agreement running from 2026.

tracks.name: Shanghai International Circuit
tracks.summary: Tilke-designed circuit whose layout echoes the Chinese character 'shang'; host of the Chinese Grand Prix with a long back straight.
tracks.article:
## Origins
The Shanghai International Circuit was built to bring Formula One to China. Constructed on reclaimed marshland in the Jiading District north of the city — ground so soft that a raft of concrete piles had to be sunk to carry the track — it was designed by Hermann Tilke and opened in 2004. Its plan was drawn to echo the Chinese character 上 (shang), the first character of the city's name, and on completion it ranked among the most expensive circuits ever built.

## The circuit
At 5.451 kilometres and 16 turns, the circuit opens with one of the sport's most distinctive sequences: a long, ever-tightening right-hand spiral through Turns 1 and 2 that winds down to a slow left, forcing a constantly decreasing radius under braking. Its signature feature is the enormous back straight before Turn 14 — roughly 1.2 kilometres of full throttle feeding into a hard hairpin, which forms one of the calendar's main overtaking zones. A high-speed complex at Turns 7 and 8 tests commitment through the middle of the lap.

## Racing at Shanghai
The circuit has been the permanent home of the Chinese Grand Prix throughout the event's history, Rubens Barrichello winning the inaugural race for Ferrari in 2004. The Grand Prix ran annually through 2019 before the pandemic and its aftermath kept Formula One away from 2020 to 2023; it returned in 2024 and remains on the calendar for 2026, once again as a sprint round. Lewis Hamilton has been the venue's most successful driver, with six wins. The long back straight and heavy braking zones have kept the circuit a regular source of close racing.

tracks.name: Autodrom Most
tracks.summary: A circuit in the northwest of the Czech Republic used by World Superbikes and other series.

tracks.name: Automotodrom Brno
tracks.summary: The Masaryk Circuit at Brno, a flowing, undulating circuit in the Czech Republic (opened 1987). A long-standing host of the Czech motorcycle Grand Prix, it returned to the MotoGP calendar in 2025 after a five-year absence.
tracks.article:
## Origins
Racing at Brno dates back to 1930, when a Grand Prix circuit was laid out on public roads through the hills and villages south-west of the Moravian city and named the Masaryk Circuit after Tomáš Garrigue Masaryk, the first president of Czechoslovakia. That original road course was vast — close to 30 kilometres in its earliest form — and was progressively shortened over the following decades. The modern permanent Automotodrom, built within the footprint of the old circuit, opened in 1987 and replaced public-road racing with a purpose-built facility.

## The circuit
The permanent circuit is 5.403 kilometres long with 14 turns, and its defining quality is topography. Laid across a hillside, it climbs and drops throughout the lap, its wide surface carrying a series of long, cambered corners linked by gradient changes that reward carried speed. The sweeping, undulating layout — fast downhill sections braking into hard corners — has long made it popular with riders and a circuit where slipstreaming and late braking shape motorcycle racing.

## Racing at Brno
Brno's central event has long been the Czech round of the motorcycle world championship, held regularly at the permanent circuit from 1987 and tracing its lineage to Grand Prix racing on the old Masaryk Circuit decades earlier. The track has also hosted the Superbike World Championship at various points and the World Touring Car Championship between 2006 and 2011. After the 2020 race the Grand Prix dropped off the MotoGP calendar for five years amid funding and resurfacing concerns, returning in 2025; it remains on the schedule through 2029 under a multi-year agreement.

tracks.name: Rally Finland
tracks.summary: Fast gravel rally based around Jyvaskyla, famed for huge crests and jumps; often called the 'Grand Prix of rallying'.

tracks.name: Bugatti Circuit (Le Mans)
tracks.summary: Permanent circuit sharing its start-finish and pits with the Le Mans 24 Hours course; hosts the French motorcycle Grand Prix and held the 1967 F1 French GP.
tracks.article:
## Origins
The Bugatti Circuit was built by the Automobile Club de l'Ouest, organiser of the Le Mans 24 Hours, as a permanent facility that could operate year-round independently of the long endurance circuit. Opened in 1965 and named after Ettore Bugatti, it was laid out at the Le Mans complex, sharing the pit buildings and the start-finish straight — the stretch passing beneath the Dunlop bridge — with the Circuit de la Sarthe before turning off into its own tighter, self-contained loop.

## The circuit
At 4.185 kilometres over 14 turns, the Bugatti Circuit uses the opening part of the 24 Hours course — the run to the Dunlop chicane and the curve at La Chapelle — before diverging into a compact infield of slower corners, among them the Garage Vert complex, and rejoining the main straight. The result is a stop-start layout of heavy braking and second- and third-gear corners: technical and demanding, but without the long, flowing sections of the full Le Mans circuit.

## Racing at Le Mans
The Bugatti Circuit's best-known regular event is the French motorcycle Grand Prix, which it has hosted for many years as a fixture of the Grand Prix motorcycle season. Its Formula One history, by contrast, amounts to a single race: the 1967 French Grand Prix, won by reigning world champion Jack Brabham in a car of his own construction, ahead of team-mate Denny Hulme. The tight infield was poorly received, and Formula One never returned, leaving the 1967 event as the circuit's sole World Championship Grand Prix.

tracks.name: Circuit de Nevers Magny-Cours
tracks.summary: Central French circuit rebuilt in 1991, home of the French Grand Prix from 1991 to 2008.
tracks.article:
## Origins
The circuit at Magny-Cours, in the rural Nièvre department of central France, opened in 1960 and spent its early decades as a modest venue best known for the Winfield racing school before falling into decline. Its transformation was political: Nièvre was the home region of President François Mitterrand, and in 1986 the departmental government bought the track with the express aim of taking the French Grand Prix from the Circuit Paul Ricard in the south. Rebuilt almost from scratch with public funding, the modernised circuit reopened in 1991 with what was widely regarded as the smoothest surface in Formula One.

## The circuit
The 4.411-kilometre lap runs to 17 turns across notably flat terrain, and several of its corners were named after and modelled on famous curves elsewhere: the fast Estoril corner, the tight Adelaide hairpin, and chicanes evoking the Nürburgring and Imola. The very smooth asphalt was gentle on tyres, but the layout's mix of slow hairpins and tight chicanes made overtaking difficult, giving the circuit a reputation for processional racing that qualifying and strategy often decided.

## Racing at Magny-Cours
Magny-Cours hosted the French Grand Prix for eighteen consecutive years, from 1991 to 2008, Nigel Mansell winning the first running for Williams-Renault. It was the last French circuit to hold a round of the Formula One World Championship until the race's later, brief revival at Paul Ricard. The venue has also been a long-running host of the Superbike World Championship, which it continues to hold alongside sports-car and GT events.

tracks.name: Circuit de Pau-Ville
tracks.summary: Classic street circuit through the town of Pau, host of the Pau Grand Prix since 1933 and long a Formula 2 and Formula 3000 fixture.

tracks.name: Circuit de Reims-Gueux
tracks.summary: Fast triangular road circuit near Reims that hosted the French Grand Prix several times in the 1950s and early 1960s; its pit buildings still stand. It hosted the French Grand Prix until 1966.

tracks.name: Circuit Paul Ricard
tracks.summary: Le Castellet circuit known for its distinctive blue-and-red run-off; hosted the French Grand Prix and remains a major testing venue.

tracks.name: Dijon-Prenois
tracks.summary: Short, hilly Burgundy circuit remembered for the 1979 Villeneuve-Arnoux duel; hosted French and Swiss Grands Prix.

tracks.name: Rouen-Les-Essarts
tracks.summary: Sweeping downhill road circuit south of Rouen that held the French Grand Prix five times between 1952 and 1968.

tracks.name: AVUS
tracks.summary: Berlin circuit of two long straights joined by a steeply banked north curve; hosted the 1959 German Grand Prix and is now part of a motorway.

tracks.name: Erftlandring (Kerpen-Manheim)
tracks.summary: A historic kart circuit at Kerpen-Manheim near Cologne, the home track of the Schumacher brothers, where Ayrton Senna and a young Mika Häkkinen also raced.

tracks.name: Hockenheimring
tracks.summary: A fast circuit in the Rhine valley forests near Heidelberg, Germany, famous for its vast stadium section. It was the long-time home of the German Grand Prix, which it last hosted in 2019, and now headlines the DTM.

tracks.name: Lausitzring
tracks.summary: Multi-purpose German complex combining a tri-oval with infield road courses; site of a near-fatal (Alex Zanardi survived) 2001 CART crash and now a DTM and test venue.

tracks.name: Nurburgring (GP-Strecke)
tracks.summary: The modern Grand Prix circuit at the Nürburgring in Germany (opened 1984), built alongside the legendary Nordschleife. A former Formula 1 venue — it hosted the German, European and Luxembourg Grands Prix, most recently the 2020 Eifel Grand Prix — and today runs endurance and national racing.

tracks.name: Nurburgring Nordschleife
tracks.summary: The 'Green Hell', a 20+ km Eifel loop with over 150 corners; former F1 venue and home of the Nurburgring 24 Hours.

tracks.name: ProKart Raceland Wackersdorf
tracks.summary: Professional CIK-FIA kart facility in Bavaria with indoor and outdoor tracks; host of FIA Karting World Championship rounds.

tracks.name: Rallye Deutschland
tracks.summary: A rally on the tarmac vineyards roads and Baumholder military ranges around Trier. A World Rally Championship round from 2002 to 2019; Germany’s WRC slot is now filled by the Central European Rally.

tracks.name: Sachsenring
tracks.summary: Compact, anti-clockwise Saxon circuit, home of the German motorcycle Grand Prix; the modern permanent track dates from 1996.

tracks.name: Acropolis Rally
tracks.summary: One of the toughest events in rallying, run on rough, rocky, dusty mountain tracks in the Greek summer heat.

tracks.name: Hungaroring
tracks.summary: Twisty circuit near Budapest that hosted the first Formula One race behind the Iron Curtain in 1986.

tracks.name: Buddh International Circuit
tracks.summary: A modern Hermann Tilke circuit near Delhi, India (opened 2011). It hosted the Formula 1 Indian Grand Prix from 2011 to 2013 and held the inaugural — and to date only — Indian MotoGP round in 2023; neither championship currently races there.

tracks.name: Mandalika International Street Circuit
tracks.summary: Coastal circuit in the Mandalika resort on Lombok that brought the Indonesian motorcycle Grand Prix back in 2022.

tracks.name: 7 Laghi Kart
tracks.summary: International kart circuit at Castelletto di Branduzzo in the province of Pavia, set within a large lakeside complex.

tracks.name: Adria Karting Raceway
tracks.summary: Modern CIK-FIA kart track in the Veneto, part of the Adria International Raceway complex, with wide run-off areas.

tracks.name: Autodromo Enzo e Dino Ferrari (Imola)
tracks.summary: Fast, undulating anti-clockwise circuit at Imola, Italy (opened 1953), scene of the 1994 tragedies that killed Ayrton Senna and Roland Ratzenberger. It returned to Formula 1 in 2020 and hosted the Emilia-Romagna Grand Prix through 2025, before dropping off the calendar for 2026.

tracks.name: Autodromo Nazionale Monza
tracks.summary: One of the oldest purpose-built circuits in the world and the historic 'Temple of Speed' home of the Italian Grand Prix.

tracks.name: Circuito Internazionale Napoli (Sarno)
tracks.summary: Long-standing international kart circuit at Sarno near Naples, in the shadow of Mount Vesuvius; a regular CIK-FIA and Italian championship venue.

tracks.name: Franciacorta Karting Track
tracks.summary: A modern kart circuit at Castrezzato near Brescia, opened in 2020, host of the FIA Karting World Championship (2023 and 2024) and the KZ World Cup (2025). It is a separate facility from the nearby Franciacorta autodrome.

tracks.name: Mugello Circuit
tracks.summary: Flowing, hilly Tuscan circuit owned by Ferrari; a beloved MotoGP venue for the Italian motorcycle Grand Prix.

tracks.name: Pescara Circuit
tracks.summary: Enormous triangular road circuit on the Adriatic coast; at over 25 km the longest track ever to host a World Championship Grand Prix (1957).

tracks.name: Rally Italia Sardegna
tracks.summary: Italy's round of the World Rally Championship on the narrow, dusty, technical gravel roads of Sardinia.

tracks.name: South Garda Karting
tracks.summary: Prestigious kart circuit at Lonato del Garda that hosts CIK-FIA World Championship rounds; a proving ground for future F1 stars.

tracks.name: Fuji Speedway
tracks.summary: Toyota-owned circuit beneath Mount Fuji with a very long main straight; hosted the Japanese Grand Prix and a round of the World Endurance Championship.

tracks.name: Mobility Resort Motegi (Twin Ring Motegi)
tracks.summary: The Japanese circuit at Motegi (renamed Mobility Resort Motegi in 2022), a technical stop-and-go road course that hosts the Japanese motorcycle Grand Prix. Its separate superspeedway oval — which held the IndyCar Indy Japan 300 from 1998 to 2011 — has since been decommissioned.

tracks.name: Okayama International Circuit
tracks.summary: Technical circuit formerly known as TI Circuit Aida that hosted the Formula One Pacific Grand Prix in 1994 and 1995.

tracks.name: Rally Japan
tracks.summary: Japan’s round of the World Rally Championship. The event first ran in 2004 on the gravel roads of Hokkaido, and was revived in 2022 as a tarmac rally based in the Aichi and Gifu regions around Toyota City.

tracks.name: Suzuka International Racing Course
tracks.summary: Honda-owned figure-eight circuit widely regarded as one of the greatest drivers' tracks; home of the Japanese Grand Prix and Suzuka 8 Hours.

tracks.name: Safari Rally
tracks.summary: Legendary rough, long-distance African rally, historically based around Nairobi and now Naivasha, testing cars against terrain and wildlife.

tracks.name: Guia Circuit
tracks.summary: Narrow, demanding street circuit around Guia Hill, home of the Macau Grand Prix and its famed Formula 3 and touring-car races.

tracks.name: Sepang International Circuit
tracks.summary: Sepang International Circuit near Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia — Hermann Tilke's first major Formula 1 project (opened 1999). It hosted the Malaysian Grand Prix from 1999 to 2017 and today hosts the Malaysian motorcycle Grand Prix (MotoGP).

tracks.name: Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez
tracks.summary: High-altitude Mexico City circuit whose stadium section around the old Peraltada draws huge crowds at the Mexican Grand Prix.

tracks.name: Circuit de Monaco
tracks.summary: Tight, glamorous street circuit through Monte Carlo and the crown jewel of the Formula One calendar since 1950.

tracks.name: Circuit Zandvoort
tracks.summary: Seaside dunes circuit that returned to the Formula One calendar in 2021 with banked corners for the Dutch Grand Prix.

tracks.name: TT Circuit Assen
tracks.summary: TT Circuit Assen in the Netherlands — 'The Cathedral' of motorcycle racing, host of the Dutch TT every year since 1949 bar the COVID-cancelled 2020 round.

tracks.name: Algarve International Circuit (Portimao)
tracks.summary: Undulating roller-coaster circuit at Portimao that hosts the Portuguese motorcycle Grand Prix and held the F1 Portuguese GP in 2020 and 2021.

tracks.name: Autodromo do Estoril
tracks.summary: Circuit near Lisbon that hosted the Portuguese Grand Prix from 1984 to 1996, including Ayrton Senna's first F1 win.

tracks.name: Rally de Portugal
tracks.summary: Fast, sandy gravel rally now based in the north around Matosinhos, one of the best-attended events on the WRC calendar.

tracks.name: Lusail International Circuit
tracks.summary: Floodlit circuit near Doha built for MotoGP in 2004 that added the Qatar Grand Prix to the Formula One calendar in 2021.

tracks.name: Jeddah Corniche Circuit
tracks.summary: An exceptionally fast street circuit along the Red Sea corniche in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia — billed as the fastest street circuit in Formula 1 and one of the longest, with 27 corners.

tracks.name: Marina Bay Street Circuit
tracks.summary: Downtown street circuit that hosted Formula One's first night race in 2008; reconfigured to 19 turns from 2023.

tracks.name: Kyalami Circuit
tracks.summary: High-veld circuit near Johannesburg that hosted the South African Grand Prix and remains the country's premier racing venue.

tracks.name: Korea International Circuit
tracks.summary: Coastal circuit near Yeongam that held the Korean Grand Prix from 2010 to 2013.

tracks.name: Circuit de Barcelona-Catalunya
tracks.summary: A modern circuit near Barcelona and long the home of the Spanish Grand Prix — renamed the Barcelona-Catalunya Grand Prix for 2026, with the Spanish GP title moving to Madrid. For years it was also Formula 1's main pre-season testing venue, before testing moved to Bahrain.

tracks.name: Circuit Ricardo Tormo
tracks.summary: Stadium-style circuit at Cheste near Valencia that traditionally closes the MotoGP season with the Valencian Community Grand Prix.

tracks.name: Circuito de Jerez - Angel Nieto
tracks.summary: Andalusian circuit that hosts the Spanish motorcycle Grand Prix and staged the Spanish and European F1 Grands Prix in the late 1980s and 1990s.

tracks.name: Circuito del Jarama
tracks.summary: Tight, twisting circuit north of Madrid that hosted nine Spanish Grands Prix between 1968 and 1981.

tracks.name: Circuito Internacional de Zuera
tracks.summary: International kart circuit north of Zaragoza in Aragon, an FIA Karting venue also used by motorcycles.

tracks.name: Montjuic Circuit
tracks.summary: Park street circuit in Barcelona whose fast, dangerous layout hosted the Spanish Grand Prix until a fatal 1975 accident ended F1 racing there.

tracks.name: MotorLand Aragon
tracks.summary: Tilke-designed circuit near Alcaniz in Aragon that hosts the Aragon motorcycle Grand Prix and World Superbike rounds.

tracks.name: Pedralbes Circuit
tracks.summary: Fast street circuit on the wide avenues of Barcelona that held the Spanish Grand Prix in 1951 and 1954.

tracks.name: Valencia Street Circuit
tracks.summary: Harbourside street circuit that hosted the European Grand Prix from 2008 to 2012, crossing a swing bridge over the marina.

tracks.name: Rally Sweden
tracks.summary: The only true winter round of the World Rally Championship, run on snow and ice with studded tyres; now based around Umea in the north.

tracks.name: Scandinavian Raceway (Anderstorp)
tracks.summary: Circuit at Anderstorp, built partly around an airfield, that hosted the Swedish Grand Prix from 1973 to 1978. It remains an active circuit for Swedish national racing and track days.

tracks.name: Circuit Bremgarten
tracks.summary: Tree-lined forest circuit near Bern that hosted the Swiss Grand Prix until circuit racing was banned in Switzerland after the 1955 Le Mans disaster.

tracks.name: Buriram International Circuit (Chang)
tracks.summary: Tilke-designed circuit in Buriram, Thailand's first FIA Grade 1 track and host of the Thailand motorcycle Grand Prix.

tracks.name: Istanbul Park
tracks.summary: A modern circuit on the Asian side of Istanbul, Turkey, famous for the multi-apex Turn 8. It hosted the Turkish Grand Prix from 2005 to 2011 and again in 2020-2021; a 2026 agreement returns Formula 1 for 2027-2031.

tracks.name: Yas Marina Circuit
tracks.summary: Abu Dhabi circuit on Yas Island, traditional season finale of the Formula One calendar and a day-to-night race.

tracks.name: Aintree Motor Racing Circuit
tracks.summary: Circuit around the Aintree horse-racing course near Liverpool that hosted the British Grand Prix five times, including Stirling Moss's 1955 home win.

tracks.name: Brands Hatch
tracks.summary: Kent circuit set in a natural amphitheatre that alternated the British Grand Prix with Silverstone into the 1980s and remains a busy national venue.

tracks.name: PF International Kart Circuit
tracks.summary: The UK's premier kart circuit at Brandon near Grantham, and the only British short-circuit track holding a CIK-FIA International A licence.

tracks.name: Rally GB (Wales)
tracks.summary: Britain’s round of the World Rally Championship until 2019, run on the forest gravel of Wales. Descended from the historic RAC Rally, one of the sport’s oldest events.

tracks.name: Rockingham Motor Speedway
tracks.summary: Corby oval-and-road complex, one of Europe's few banked speedways, that briefly hosted American CART races before closing to racing in 2018.

tracks.name: Rowrah Kart Circuit
tracks.summary: Cumbrian kart circuit laid out in a disused quarry, an early proving ground for British F1 drivers including Lewis Hamilton and George Russell.

tracks.name: Silverstone Circuit
tracks.summary: Former WWII airfield that hosted the first FIA Formula One World Championship race in 1950; permanent home of the British Grand Prix and British MotoGP.
tracks.article:
## Origins

Silverstone was built not as a racetrack but as a wartime airfield. RAF Silverstone operated as a bomber station from 1943, and when the war ended its wide runways and perimeter roads were repurposed for motor racing. The first British Grand Prix was held there in 1948, and in 1950 Silverstone staged the inaugural round of the new FIA Formula One World Championship — the first world-championship Grand Prix ever run, won by Giuseppe Farina for Alfa Romeo.

## The circuit

The modern Grand Prix layout measures 5.891 km across 18 turns and is defined by its high average speed. Its most celebrated section is the Maggotts–Becketts–Chapel sequence, a rapid series of direction changes regarded as one of the great tests of a Formula One car's high-speed balance. The long Hangar Straight, the fast entry at Copse and the heavy braking zone at Stowe complete a circuit that rewards aerodynamic stability and driver commitment.

## Racing at Silverstone

Although the British Grand Prix rotated between Silverstone, Aintree and Brands Hatch for much of the mid-20th century, it has been held at Silverstone continuously since 1987 and remains one of the best-attended races of the season. The venue also hosts the British round of MotoGP, rounds of the British Touring Car and British GT championships, and endurance racing in the European Le Mans Series. The Formula One lap record stands at 1:27.097, set by Max Verstappen for Red Bull in 2020.

tracks.name: Atlanta Motor Speedway
tracks.summary: 1.54-mile Georgia quad-oval reprofiled in 2022 with steeper banking to produce superspeedway-style pack racing.

tracks.name: Auto Club Speedway
tracks.summary: A fast, abrasive two-mile D-shaped oval in Fontana, California, long a NASCAR favourite for its worn, multi-groove racing. It held its final NASCAR Cup race in 2023 and has since been largely demolished for redevelopment.

tracks.name: Barber Motorsports Park
tracks.summary: Immaculate, park-like road course near Birmingham, Alabama, adjoining a renowned motorcycle museum; an IndyCar venue.

tracks.name: Bristol Motor Speedway
tracks.summary: Steeply banked half-mile 'bullring' in Tennessee known for its short-track intensity and colosseum-like grandstands.

tracks.name: Charlotte Motor Speedway
tracks.summary: 1.5-mile North Carolina quad-oval that hosts the Coca-Cola 600; also runs a NASCAR event on its infield 'roval'.

tracks.name: Circuit of the Americas
tracks.summary: Purpose-built Austin circuit with a steep uphill Turn 1; hosts the United States Grand Prix and the Grand Prix of the Americas MotoGP round.

tracks.name: Darlington Raceway
tracks.summary: Egg-shaped South Carolina oval, 'the track too tough to tame', where drivers earn the 'Darlington stripe' on the wall.

tracks.name: Daytona International Speedway
tracks.summary: High-banked 2.5-mile tri-oval that hosts the Daytona 500 and, on its combined road course, the Rolex 24 sports-car race.
tracks.article:
## Origins

Daytona International Speedway opened in 1959, built by NASCAR founder Bill France Sr. to replace the stock-car racing that had been held on the beach and public road at Daytona Beach. Its high-banked design was intended to allow far higher speeds than a flat oval while improving the view for spectators.

## The circuit

The main oval is 2.5 miles (4.02 km) long, with 31 degrees of banking in the turns, and introduced the "tri-oval" shape — a shallow kink on the pit straight that improved sightlines. The steep banking and long straights make Daytona a superspeedway, where cars run in tightly packed drafting formations at sustained high speed. An infield road course combines with the banking to form a 3.56-mile circuit used for sports-car racing.

## Racing at Daytona

The circuit's signature event is the Daytona 500. Unusually, NASCAR opens its season with its most prestigious race, and a win in the "Great American Race" can define a driver's career. On the road course, the Rolex 24 at Daytona has been staged since 1966 and is one of the world's major endurance events, opening the international sports-car season each January. A redevelopment between 2013 and 2016 rebuilt the grandstands around roughly 101,500 seats, reaffirming Daytona's standing as one of the most famous venues in American motorsport.

tracks.name: Detroit Street Circuit
tracks.summary: A tight downtown street circuit in Detroit, Michigan that hosted the United States Grand Prix from 1982 to 1988. (Later Detroit races moved to Belle Isle, and from 2023 to a separate downtown IndyCar circuit.)

tracks.name: Dover Motor Speedway
tracks.summary: High-banked concrete one-mile Delaware oval nicknamed the 'Monster Mile'.

tracks.name: Trackhouse Motorplex (formerly GoPro Motorplex)
tracks.summary: America's premier outdoor kart track at Mooresville, North Carolina, its layout inspired by Italy's Parma circuit.

tracks.name: Homestead-Miami Speedway
tracks.summary: A 1.5-mile oval in Homestead, Florida, whose progressive banking produces wide, multi-groove racing. It hosted NASCAR's season finale from 2002 to 2019, and the Cup Series championship finale is set to return there in 2026 under a new rotating model.

tracks.name: Indianapolis Motor Speedway
tracks.summary: The 2.5-mile 'Brickyard', home of the Indianapolis 500; its infield road course hosted the United States Grand Prix from 2000 to 2007.

tracks.name: Kansas Speedway
tracks.summary: 1.5-mile progressive-banking oval near Kansas City hosting NASCAR and, previously, IndyCar races.

tracks.name: Las Vegas Strip Circuit
tracks.summary: Night street circuit running along the Las Vegas Strip, revived F1 racing in the city in 2023 with a high-speed straight past the casinos.

tracks.name: Lime Rock Park
tracks.summary: Short, fast, scenic road course in the hills of northwestern Connecticut, one of America's oldest continuously operating tracks.

tracks.name: Long Beach Street Circuit
tracks.summary: Downtown Long Beach street circuit that hosted the United States Grand Prix West from 1976 to 1983 and is now IndyCar's premier street race.

tracks.name: Martinsville Speedway
tracks.summary: The shortest and oldest track on the NASCAR Cup calendar, a paper-clip-shaped half-mile in Virginia.

tracks.name: Miami International Autodrome
tracks.summary: Temporary circuit laid out around Hard Rock Stadium in Miami Gardens, host of the Miami Grand Prix since 2022.

tracks.name: Michelin Raceway Road Atlanta
tracks.summary: Undulating Georgia road course near Braselton, home of the Petit Le Mans endurance race.

tracks.name: Michigan International Speedway
tracks.summary: Wide, fast 2-mile D-shaped oval in Michigan that produces some of NASCAR's highest sustained speeds.

tracks.name: Mid-Ohio Sports Car Course
tracks.summary: Tight, hilly road course near Lexington, Ohio, a regular stop for IndyCar and sports-car racing.

tracks.name: Milwaukee Mile
tracks.summary: Flat one-mile Wisconsin oval reputed to be the oldest continuously operating motor speedway in the world.

tracks.name: New Castle Motorsports Park
tracks.summary: Major American kart racing facility east of Indianapolis, founded by former IndyCar driver Mark Dismore; host of national karting championships.

tracks.name: New Hampshire Motor Speedway
tracks.summary: Flat one-mile 'Magic Mile' oval in Loudon, the largest sports facility in New England.

tracks.name: Phoenix Raceway
tracks.summary: A one-mile, low-banked oval in Avondale, Arizona, a NASCAR staple with a distinctive dogleg. It hosted the Cup Series championship finale from 2020 to 2025; from 2026 the finale rotates between tracks (Homestead-Miami in 2026), with Phoenix keeping its two Cup dates.

tracks.name: Pikes Peak International Hill Climb
tracks.summary: The 'Race to the Clouds', a paved hill climb up Pikes Peak in Colorado climbing to 4,300 m with 156 corners and no run-off.

tracks.name: Pocono Raceway
tracks.summary: Triangular 2.5-mile Pennsylvania 'Tricky Triangle' with three distinct corners each modeled on a different circuit.

tracks.name: Richmond Raceway
tracks.summary: Three-quarter-mile D-shaped Virginia oval often called 'America's premier short track' for its side-by-side racing.

tracks.name: Road America
tracks.summary: A fast, sweeping four-mile natural-terrain road course at Elkhart Lake, Wisconsin (opened 1955) — one of America's classic circuits, home to IndyCar and IMSA sportscar rounds.

tracks.name: Sebring International Raceway
tracks.summary: Bumpy former WWII airfield circuit in Florida, home of the 12 Hours of Sebring since 1952.

tracks.name: Sonoma Raceway
tracks.summary: A hilly road course in California's Sonoma wine country, known for its elevation changes and its NASCAR Cup road race; IndyCar also raced here through 2018.

tracks.name: Streets of St. Petersburg
tracks.summary: Florida waterfront street circuit that uses part of an airport runway; traditional season opener for IndyCar.

tracks.name: Talladega Superspeedway
tracks.summary: At 2.66 miles the largest and fastest oval in NASCAR, famous for high-speed pack racing in Alabama.

tracks.name: Texas Motor Speedway
tracks.summary: A high-banked 1.5-mile oval near Fort Worth, Texas, known for fast, multi-groove NASCAR racing. IndyCar also raced here through 2023.

tracks.name: Virginia International Raceway
tracks.summary: Rolling road course on the Virginia-North Carolina border, a popular sports-car and club-racing venue.

tracks.name: Watkins Glen International
tracks.summary: Upstate New York road course that hosted the United States Grand Prix from 1961 to 1980 and remains a NASCAR and sports-car venue.

tracks.name: WeatherTech Raceway Laguna Seca
tracks.summary: California circuit near Monterey famed for the plunging, blind 'Corkscrew' esses; former MotoGP and current IndyCar venue.
